title: Films that were hailed as masterpieces upon release, and are still hailed as masterpieces today.

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

Cross-reference major award winners with frequent entries on GOAT lists. That Venn diagram is the answer to your question. You'll find films like The Godfather, Lawrence of Arabia, On the Waterfront, etc.

There are, of course, many many examples to choose from 

The first one that comes to mind for me is *Citizen Kane*. Its release was a bit overshadowed by controversy and bad press from William Randall Hearst and his media machine, but many of the critics who could give it an honest review went nuts for it. [The Variety review](https://variety.com/1941/film/reviews/citizen-kane-1200413671/) basically said this movie is wholly original and going to influence other movies from here on out. 

True of course. 

*Pulp Fiction* is another in a similar vein. Maybe even more so because it was critically and commercially successful. *Reservoir Dogs* was met with “this guy is one to watch” and *Pulp* was like, “YUP!”  And there isn’t much difference between how Tarantino was written about then and how he was written about later (like in books like *Down and Dirty Pictures*) except for perspective on how that influence played out.

IMO, that’s a question that can never be answered. For instance: “what about the films that had extraordinary acclaim when made, and years/decades later are still revered as timeless masterpieces?”

Are we talking about the public reception or the critical consensus? Are we saying the critical acclaim was unanimous upon the release because Rotten Tomatoes can only go back so far when compiling everything that was published at the time? Also, sometimes a film can be hailed a masterpiece in the context of the filmography of its director. Or a film could be embraced in a certain context (European film festivals, for instance) and rejected in another (American mainstream circles).

In my opinion, there are very few examples of films that were trashed upon release, but years later reevaluated and acclaimed as masterpieces. One that comes to mind is Roger Ebert reviewing Blade Runner: that's a case of an individual going over a film considering the context of time and impact. 

Ebert is a good indication of how mainstream American audiences welcomed certain films, and how they changed over time.

Friedkin's Sorcerer, Carpenter's The Thing, The Night of the Hunter, Pressburger and Powell's Peeping Tom, Touch of Evil, Arthur Penn's Bonnie and Clyde, Vertigo and Psycho. 

All were panned, most were forgotten for quite some time until they were reevaluated.

Of course it's difficult to metric a film's reception, on both critical and popular circles. All I'm asking is the general consensus, just a superficial analysis. 

Gene Siskel enjoyed The Thing when it was released, he thought it was a good movie and nothing else. Today, it's the highest-rated horror movie on Letterboxd and it was just featured on Sight & Sound 2022.

Bonnie and Clyde was praised by Pauline Kael. Other films were reevaluated based on the filmmaker's status in the American industry. The general consensus is completely subjective based on what you're considering.

Most of the films I know were instant classic are from the 90s and 00s. Idk if they’re old enough to truly see how time can change opinions. Still…

• Schindlers List was an event film. It was similar to Oppenheimer in the sense that you had to see it. By many it’s considered Spielbergs best film and it was hailed as his most mature work at the time. 

• No Country For Old Men was immediately proclaimed as a masterpiece. Its reputation still persists. 

• The Matrix, depends on the circles you’d focus on, but as far as genre filmmaking goes this one changed blockbusters and genre filmmaking forever. It was an instant classic and it continues to be respected.

• The Dark Knight similarly to The Matrix, its impact was immediate. At this point it’s a discussion beaten to the ground, but it’s the film responsible for the 10 film noms at the Oscars (for better or worse). It was a classic then and it continues to be today. 

• Goodfellas was heralded as the gangster film to challenge The Godfather. To many it was better. I think that speaks to its immediate success. 

• Titanic was an event film as well. Everyone and their grandmother had seen this film. It evoked old Hollywood not only in its scope and story, but in its reaction. I don’t think a romance film had been this loved since Gone with The Wind, it was really wild. Ebert proclaimed it a masterpiece in his re-review in 2011. Again, an instant classic and it persists today.

> Schindlers List was an event film. It was similar to Oppenheimer in the sense that you had to see it. By many it’s considered Spielbergs best film and it was hailed as his most mature work at the time.

I hate how low this movie shows up on listicles and discussions about 'best' films. Yeah, it's not rewatchable. At all. It's not fun to talk about. Discussions about the craft get overshadowed by the content. 

But this movie... this movie...when you were there when you came out, you know. It's understandable that it's now largely relegated to Social Studies classrooms, but it's also a crying shame. Because it's so good at doing what it does, it's easy to overlook how good it is at doing what it does.

> Bonnie and Clyde was praised by Pauline Kael.

I also think this is a bad example. A lot of critics didn't like *Bonnie and Clyde*, true, but a lot of them absolutely loved it. Ebert loved it too.

It was a huge commercial success. It was nominated for 9 Academy Awards. It was a hit by any metric.

Yeah, basically you can pick every Best Picture winner or nominee that was liked by audiences too and it still liked and you have plenty of films that meet OP's criterias.

The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938) was acclaimed on release. Here are some contemporary reviews:

[https://variety.com/1937/film/reviews/the-adventures-of-robin-hood-1200411570/#](https://variety.com/1937/film/reviews/the-adventures-of-robin-hood-1200411570/#)!

[https://archive.org/details/harrisonsreports20harr/page/n89/mode/2up?view=theater&q=robin+hood](https://archive.org/details/harrisonsreports20harr/page/n89/mode/2up?view=theater&q=robin+hood)

It currently has [100% on Rotten Tomatoes](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/1000355-adventures_of_robin_hood) from 51 reviews. Some of their modern quotes call it "The archetypal Hollywood swashbuckler" and "beyond criticism".

I've just been watching it, I'm only 30 minutes in but already there's been an action scene where Robin Hood (Errol Flynn) escapes from a banquet fighting off dozens of enemies and the action totally holds up, it's terrific, it's as well done as any such scenes I've seen in more modern films. It leads me to wonder if this film set the standard for that sort of thing.

On the more populist end of the scale, The Lord Of The Rings. The first one was a little divisive at first because of the open ended nature of it, but by the time the third one rolled around the world was primed for it, and the general consensus was that the trilogy overall delivered. Which is *still* the general consensus.

It might be a little early to say, but Fury Road is probably another one.

Mullholland Drive comes to mind. When it came out it was a huge critical success and immediately considered by many to be Lynch’s best work. 22 years later and it’s still considered a masterpiece and one of the best movies of the 21st century by many.

> Films exist to show the world how it is…

Says who? 

But really, I feel you’re judging Schindler’s List for the entertainment that it is. Film (and most art) is, in fact, entertainment. It will never be the real thing. I suppose that’s an inherent flaw in every film. To me, the most a film of that nature can do is to have some depth (which I believe it does) and approach some kernel of truth. Which I believe it does as well. 

I’d suggest to go watch Shoah instead. A documentary centered on the history of the holocaust. Still, that is a documentary made by a person with an objective. Even that can be argued that it’ll never capture the true horror of the holocaust. The point being, that art will never be real life or be able to capture it entirely.
If the mods deleted this post because it's another one of the "What is a list of movies?" posts that comprises 90% or /r/movies content, and has plagued this sub more and more recently, then Bravo!

How is Schindler’s List, The Pianist, or any other telling of the Holocaust exploitive? Should we only express it abstractly? Do you think there’s any value in dramatizing a historic event that some people not might be familiar with, or understand the scope of?

Brilliant people don’t make up words, or at least when they do it’s usually more clever than “aestheticization”
Exactly. Can you imagine a film like this having that type of cultural importance and reverberation today? "You made out during *Killers of the Flower Moon*??!!" just doesn't have the same zip.
